\chapter{Five Words for Making a Journey}
\label{ch:el-tren-y-la-playa}
\hlchaptermodality{400}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say el tren, el vuelo, el aparcamiento, el abono and la playa, and use them to plan a journey.}

Complete ES-C400-playa: choose transport, name its practical details, and say where the journey ends.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el tren]{el tren — a line drawn along}

\label{lesson:ES-C400-tren}



\begin{quote}
Say both words from the last chapter for \emph{good-looking}. (\emph{Bonito; guapo}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el coche — another way to travel on land.
  \item la estación — where this one waits.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{TREN}, one compact beat. Tap the \emph{r} once and finish with \emph{n}. Keep that ending audible: \textbf{tren} is a train; \textbf{tres} is three. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el tren} — \textquotedblleft{}the train.\textquotedblright{}

Spanish borrowed the word from French \textbf{train}. The French noun belongs to \textbf{traîner}, \textquotedblleft{}to draw, drag, or pull along.\textquotedblright{} Before rails, the central picture was already a line of connected things following one another because the front one pulled the rest. A railway made that old picture literal in iron.

English borrowed the same French noun. That is why a railway \emph{train}, a bridal \emph{train}, and a \emph{train of thought} all keep the same shape: one thing following another in a connected line.

Now make the contrast the lesson, because the mock requires this word and the book already owns its near-neighbour:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{el tren} — the train;
  \item \textbf{tres trenes} — three trains.
\end{itemize}

The last sound carries the distinction: \emph{-n} against \emph{-s}. Do not guess from context when your ear can learn the difference directly.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name rail transport and keep \emph{tren} separate from \emph{tres}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el tren}
  \item \emph{tres trenes}
  \item \emph{voy en tren}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did French \emph{traîner} mean? (\emph{To draw or drag along}.) What single sound separates \emph{tren} from \emph{tres}? (\emph{Final n versus final s}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el vuelo]{el vuelo — the journey made by flying}

\label{lesson:ES-C400-vuelo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the train}, then recall both recent words for \emph{good-looking}. (\emph{El tren; bonito; guapo}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el aeropuerto — where a flight begins.
  \item el destino — where it is going.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{VUE-lo}, two beats, with \emph{ue} joined into one quick \emph{weh}. Spanish \emph{v} and \emph{b} belong to the same sound pattern: after a pause the lips meet, while between vowels they usually soften. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el vuelo} — \textquotedblleft{}the flight.\textquotedblright{}

The noun sits beside \textbf{volar}, \textquotedblleft{}to fly,\textquotedblright{} from Latin \textbf{volāre}. The oldest meaning is the act of flying. Travel language narrows it neatly: the dictionary's third sense is the route an aeroplane covers, with or without stops, between its point of origin and its destination.

That definition gives you a useful frame rather than an isolated label:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{el vuelo sale del aeropuerto} — the flight leaves the airport;
  \item \textbf{el destino del vuelo} — the flight's destination.
\end{itemize}

English \textbf{volatile} belongs to the same Latin family. Before it meant chemically quick to evaporate or emotionally changeable, it described what could fly away. The common picture is movement into the air.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name the air journey itself: \emph{el vuelo}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el vuelo}
  \item \emph{el destino del vuelo}
  \item \emph{el tren o el vuelo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which verb stands behind \emph{vuelo}? (\emph{Volar}, to fly.) In travel, what does \emph{vuelo} name? (\emph{The route an aeroplane covers from origin to destination}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el aparcamiento]{el aparcamiento — the place built from a verb}

\label{lesson:ES-C400-aparcamiento}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the flight}. (\emph{El vuelo}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el coche — what goes here.
  \item el parque — the word inside the verb.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-par-ca-MIEN-to}, five beats, with the weight on \emph{mien}. The \emph{c} before \emph{a} is hard, and \emph{ie} stays together in one beat. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el aparcamiento} — \textquotedblleft{}parking\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}the car park.\textquotedblright{}

The pieces are transparent once you see them. \textbf{Aparcar} is \textquotedblleft{}to park,\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{-miento} turns an action into its result or place. So \emph{aparcamiento} can be the act of parking or the place set aside for it.

The tempting origin story is wrong in a useful way. Spanish \emph{aparcar} was not lifted directly from English \textbf{park} when cars arrived. The Academy derives it from Spanish \textbf{parque}. The verb first meant placing vehicles or equipment in a designated park or camp; the modern car sense grew from that Spanish family.

You will also see \textbf{parking} on signs, and across the Americas \textbf{estacionamiento}, \textbf{parqueadero}, and \textbf{parqueo} are common. This lesson teaches \emph{aparcamiento} because that is the exam's form, not because it is the only Spanish word in use.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can ask about the place for a car: \emph{el aparcamiento}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el aparcamiento}
  \item \emph{el aparcamiento del hotel}
  \item \emph{el coche está en el aparcamiento}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two pieces of \emph{aparcamiento}? (\emph{Aparcar} plus \emph{-miento}.) Where does the Academy derive \emph{aparcar} from? (\emph{Spanish parque}, not a direct borrowing of English \emph{park}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el abono]{el abono — a right you can carry}

\label{lesson:ES-C400-abono}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the car park}. (\emph{El aparcamiento}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el metro — one service a pass can cover.
  \item el euro — how its price may be shown.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-BO-no}, three beats, weighted in the middle. The \emph{b} between vowels is soft: the lips approach without a hard burst. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el abono} — \textquotedblleft{}the pass,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the season ticket,\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}the subscription.\textquotedblright{}

The dictionary keeps two nouns spelled \textbf{abono} apart. One belongs to \emph{abonar} in the sense of paying or improving soil, so it can mean a payment or fertilizer. The other belongs to \textbf{abonarse}, \textquotedblleft{}to subscribe.\textquotedblright{} It names the right a subscriber acquires and the document or set of tickets that proves that right.

Travel uses the second word:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{un abono de transporte} — a public-transport pass;
  \item \textbf{un abono mensual} — a monthly pass.
\end{itemize}

Context is doing real work. At a metro ticket machine, \emph{abono} is not compost; in a garden shop, it probably is. One spelling can hold two histories, and the noun beside it tells you which one you have.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name a pass that buys repeated use of a service: \emph{el abono}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el abono}
  \item \emph{un abono mensual}
  \item \emph{un abono de transporte}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a travel \emph{abono} prove? (\emph{A subscriber's right to use a service}.) What other everyday meaning shares the spelling? (\emph{Fertilizer}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la playa]{la playa — the flat shore at the journey's end}

\label{lesson:ES-C400-playa}



\begin{quote}
Name the four travel words so far. (\emph{El tren, el vuelo, el aparcamiento, el abono}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el mar — the water beside it.
  \item las vacaciones — when the mock sends you there.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PLA-ya}, two beats, weighted first. Finish with the consonant sound in English \emph{yes}. That keeps it apart from \textbf{plaza}, whose final consonant is \emph{th} in most of Spain and \emph{s} across most of the Americas. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la playa} — \textquotedblleft{}the beach.\textquotedblright{}

It comes from Late Latin \textbf{plagia}, a flat stretch of shore. The dictionary's first definition keeps both pieces: the edge of the sea or a large river, formed by sand on a surface that is nearly level.

Across parts of South America the old flat-open-ground idea widened beyond the water. A \textbf{playa de estacionamiento} can be an open parking area. That is not a new unrelated word; it is the same flat expanse put to another use.

Now keep the required contrast visible:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{la playa} — the beach;
  \item \textbf{la plaza} — the square.
\end{itemize}

The words differ at one place, and that place matters. Do not drop either word; say the pair until the ending decides it before context has to rescue you.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name a beach as a destination and distinguish it from a town square.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la playa}
  \item \emph{la playa, la plaza}
  \item \emph{voy a la playa en tren}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Late Latin \emph{plagia} name? (\emph{A flat stretch of shore}.) Which sound separates \emph{playa} from \emph{plaza}? (\emph{Y from z or s}.) Then name the whole travel set. (\emph{El tren, el vuelo, el aparcamiento, el abono, la playa}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
